content.tagline: Mountains at the heart of Asia
content.overview:
High in the middle of Asia, Afghanistan is a landlocked country of snowy mountains, dusty plains and green river valleys. It borders Pakistan, Iran, Turkmenistan, Uzbekistan, Tajikistan and, along a thin finger of land called the Wakhan Corridor, China. At roughly 652,000 km² it is slightly smaller than Texas, and about 40 million people live there. The capital, Kabul, sits in a bowl of mountains nearly 1,800 meters above sea level.

For thousands of years, Afghanistan was a crossroads where traders, armies and ideas passed between Persia, India and Central Asia along the Silk Road. That history left behind a mix of peoples, including Pashtuns, Tajiks, Hazaras and Uzbeks, who speak Dari, Pashto, Turkmen and other languages.

Most Afghans live in villages and farm wheat, fruit and nuts, though Kabul and other cities have grown quickly. Decades of war have made life hard, and since 2021 the country has been ruled by the Taliban movement.
content.landAndNature:
The Hindu Kush mountains run like a spine across the country, with peaks above 7,000 meters in the far northeast. Rivers such as the Kabul, Helmand and Amu Darya flow out of the snowfields to water valleys where farmers grow pomegranates, grapes, apricots and almonds. In the southwest lie the sandy Registan Desert and salt flats, while the north opens into rolling grassland.

Winters are bitterly cold and summers hot and dry. Snow leopards, Marco Polo sheep with huge curling horns, ibex and wolves live in the high mountains. Band-e-Amir, a chain of six deep-blue lakes held back by natural dams of mineral rock, became the country's first national park in 2009.
content.peopleAndCulture:
Dari (a form of Persian) and Pashto are the main languages, and nearly everyone is Muslim. Hospitality is a serious matter: guests are offered green tea, nuts and dried fruit the moment they arrive. Flat naan bread comes with almost every meal, and the national dish, Kabuli pulao, is rice cooked with carrots, raisins and lamb.

Afghans have flown kites for centuries, and kite fighting, where flyers try to cut each other's strings, is a beloved pastime. The traditional sport buzkashi is played on horseback, with riders wrestling for a goat carcass. Poetry is treasured; the famous poet Rumi was born near Balkh in the 1200s. Nowruz, the spring new year, is celebrated with music, picnics and the attan, a whirling circle dance.
content.history:
People have lived here for tens of thousands of years, and the region of Bactria was rich long before Alexander the Great marched through around 330 BC. Buddhism flourished later; giant Buddha statues were carved into a cliff at Bamiyan in the 500s. Islam arrived in the 600s and 700s.

The modern state began in 1747 when Ahmad Shah Durrani united the tribes. In the 1800s Britain fought three wars trying to control Afghanistan but never fully succeeded. The country was a monarchy until 1973. In 1979 the Soviet Union invaded, starting a ten-year war, followed by civil war and Taliban rule from 1996. After the attacks of September 11, 2001, a US-led coalition removed the Taliban and a republic was set up. The Taliban returned to power in 2021 when foreign troops left.
funFacts: Lapis lazuli, the deep-blue stone used in ancient Egyptian jewelry, has been mined in Afghanistan's Badakhshan province for more than 6,000 years.
The two giant Buddhas of Bamiyan, about 55 and 38 meters tall, stood for 1,400 years before the Taliban destroyed them in 2001.
Afghanistan is famous for pomegranates; the fruit from Kandahar is considered among the sweetest in the world.
The Afghan hound, a dog with long silky hair, was bred to hunt in cold mountain country.
In buzkashi, the national sport, horseback riders battle to carry a goat carcass across a goal line.
The Wakhan Corridor is so narrow that in places the country is only about 15 kilometers wide.

content.tagline: Home of the giant sable antelope
content.overview:
Angola stretches along the Atlantic coast of southwestern Africa, covering about 1.25 million square kilometers, nearly twice the size of Texas. Its capital, Luanda, is a bustling port city of high-rise towers and crowded neighborhoods that is one of the largest cities in Africa. Around 36 million people live in Angola, making it the most populous Portuguese-speaking country on the continent. A small separate piece of the country, Cabinda, lies to the north, cut off from the rest by a strip of the Democratic Republic of the Congo.

Angola is rich in oil and diamonds, and the money they bring has built gleaming office blocks in Luanda, although many Angolans still live in poverty in the countryside and in city outskirts. The country is a republic with an elected president and parliament. After decades of war that ended in 2002, Angolans have been rebuilding roads, railways, and schools, and a young population, more than half under 20, is shaping a fast-changing nation known for its music and dance.
content.landAndNature: From a narrow, dry coastal plain the land climbs steeply to a vast central highland, the planalto, where most people farm. Mount Moco, the highest point, reaches about 2,600 meters. Great rivers begin here: the Cuanza flows to the Atlantic, the Cubango wanders southeast to feed Botswana's Okavango Delta, and the mighty Congo River forms part of the northern border. In the far south the Namib Desert crosses in from Namibia, home to the welwitschia, a plant with two leathery leaves that can live for more than a thousand years. The Kalandula Falls on the Lucala River plunge over 100 meters in a wide curtain. Angola's national symbol is the giant sable antelope, with curved horns over 1.5 meters long, which was feared extinct until it was rediscovered in 2004.
content.peopleAndCulture: The largest groups are the Ovimbundu, Ambundu, and Bakongo, and languages such as Umbundu, Kimbundu, and Kikongo are spoken alongside official Portuguese. Most Angolans are Christian. A typical meal centers on funge, a smooth porridge of cassava or corn, served with muamba de galinha, chicken simmered in palm oil with okra. Angola's musical influence reaches far beyond its borders: semba, an older dance style, is an ancestor of Brazil's samba, and kizomba, a smooth partner dance from the 1980s, is now taught in dance schools worldwide. Basketball is a national strength, with the men's team winning the African championship 11 times, and the soccer team is nicknamed the Palancas Negras, the black sables.
content.history: Bantu-speaking peoples settled here over a thousand years ago and built kingdoms such as Kongo and Ndongo, whose rulers held the title ngola, the source of the country's name. Portuguese ships arrived in 1483, and Luanda was founded in 1576. For about 300 years Angola was one of the main sources of enslaved Africans shipped across the Atlantic, especially to Brazil. Queen Nzinga of Ndongo fought the Portuguese for decades in the 1600s. A war of independence began in 1961, and Portugal withdrew in 1975. Almost immediately a civil war broke out between rival movements backed by Cold War powers; it lasted 27 years, killed hundreds of thousands, and left the land littered with mines. Peace came in 2002, followed by an oil boom.
funFacts: Angola's flag shows half a cogwheel, a machete, and a star, symbols chosen when the country became independent in 1975.
The kizomba dance craze that fills clubs from Lisbon to Los Angeles began in the neighborhoods of Luanda.
The giant sable antelope survived the civil war hidden in a remote forest and was confirmed alive by camera traps in 2004.
The welwitschia of Angola's Namib Desert grows only two leaves in its entire life, which can last over a thousand years.
Kalandula Falls is about 400 meters wide, making it one of the largest waterfalls in Africa by volume.

content.tagline: Land of the eagles
content.overview:
On the western edge of the Balkan Peninsula, Albania faces Italy across the Adriatic and Ionian Seas. It is a small country, about the size of the US state of Maryland, but it packs in snowy mountains, wild rivers, olive groves, and a long coastline of turquoise bays known as the Albanian Riviera. The capital, Tirana, is famous for apartment blocks painted in bold oranges, purples, and greens, an idea launched by a mayor who was also a painter.

About 2.8 million people live in Albania, and millions more Albanians live in neighboring Kosovo, North Macedonia, Italy, and beyond. The language, Albanian, forms its own separate branch of the Indo-European family, related to no other living tongue. For most of the 20th century the country was cut off from the world under a strict communist government, but since the early 1990s it has become a parliamentary republic, joined NATO, and applied to join the European Union. Tourism is growing fast as visitors discover its beaches and mountain villages.
content.landAndNature: Roughly seven-tenths of Albania is mountainous. In the far north rise the Albanian Alps, nicknamed the Accursed Mountains for their jagged, hard-to-cross peaks, where shepherds still move flocks to high pastures each summer. The Vjosa River flows for about 270 kilometers without a single dam, which earned it protection in 2023 as Europe's first wild-river national park. Lake Ohrid, shared with North Macedonia, is more than a million years old and home to fish found nowhere else. The coast has a warm Mediterranean climate, while inland winters bring deep snow. Brown bears, wolves, and the extremely rare Balkan lynx survive in the forests, and Dalmatian pelicans nest in the Karavasta Lagoon.
content.peopleAndCulture: Albanians speak two main dialects, Gheg in the north and Tosk in the south. Most people are Muslim, with large Orthodox and Catholic Christian communities, and the country is known for religious tolerance. Hospitality is a point of honor: an old code called besa means keeping a promise and protecting guests at any cost. Meals often begin with byrek, a flaky pastry filled with cheese or spinach, and might include tavë kosi, lamb baked with yogurt. In the south, groups sing iso-polyphony, a layered style of harmony recognized by UNESCO. Soccer is the favorite sport, and strong coffee served slowly in cafés is a daily ritual. Mother Teresa, the famous nun, was ethnically Albanian.
content.history: The Illyrians lived here more than 2,000 years ago, followed by Roman and Byzantine rule. In the 1400s the national hero Gjergj Kastrioti, known as Skanderbeg, held off the Ottoman Empire for 25 years, but Albania eventually spent more than four centuries under Ottoman control. Independence was declared in 1912. After World War II, communist leader Enver Hoxha ruled from 1944 until his death in 1985. He banned religion, sealed the borders, and had roughly 170,000 concrete bunkers built in case of invasion. Communism collapsed in 1991, and hard years of poverty and emigration followed. Albania joined NATO in 2009 and has been a candidate to join the European Union since 2014.
funFacts: Albanians call their country Shqipëri, often translated as Land of the Eagles, which explains the black double-headed eagle on the red flag.
Some of the country's 170,000 Cold War bunkers have been turned into museums, cafés, and even a hostel.
In Albania, a sideways shake of the head traditionally means yes, and a nod means no, the opposite of most of Europe.
Lake Ohrid is one of the oldest lakes on Earth and holds about 200 species that live nowhere else.
The ancient city of Butrint has ruins from Greek, Roman, Byzantine, and Venetian times layered on one small peninsula.

content.tagline: A mountain microstate with two princes
content.overview:
Tucked high in the Pyrenees between France and Spain, Andorra is one of the smallest countries in the world. At 468 square kilometers it would fit inside New York City with room to spare. The capital, Andorra la Vella, sits about 1,000 meters above sea level, making it the highest capital city in Europe. Around 80,000 people live here, and most of them are not Andorran citizens but residents from Spain, Portugal, and France who came for work.

Andorra has an unusual government. It is a co-principality, meaning it has two heads of state at once: the President of France and the Catholic Bishop of Urgell in Spain. In practice a parliament called the General Council makes the laws. The official language is Catalan, the only country where that is true. Andorra earns its living from visitors, about eight million a year, who come to ski in winter, hike in summer, and shop in its tax-free stores. It uses the euro but is not a member of the European Union.
content.landAndNature: Every part of Andorra is mountainous. Three steep valleys, carved by the Valira rivers, meet at the capital, and the peaks around them top 2,900 meters at Coma Pedrosa, the highest point. Winters bring heavy snow that feeds the Grandvalira and Pal-Arinsal ski areas, while summers are mild and sunny. Dozens of small glacial lakes, called estanys, sit in high rocky basins above forests of pine and fir. Chamois, a nimble mountain goat-antelope, leap across cliffs, marmots whistle from the meadows, and golden eagles and huge bearded vultures circle overhead. The Madriu-Perafita-Claror Valley, a quiet glacial valley with no road at all, is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
content.peopleAndCulture: Catalan is the official language, but Spanish, Portuguese, and French are heard everywhere, and many children grow up speaking three or four languages. Traditional dishes reflect hard mountain winters: trinxat is a hearty mash of potato, cabbage, and bacon, and escudella is a thick stew of meat, beans, and pasta served at winter festivals. On the night of the summer solstice, young people carry blazing torches down the mountainsides in the falles, a fire festival recognized by UNESCO. Tiny Romanesque stone churches with slender bell towers, some nearly a thousand years old, dot the villages. Skiing is the national sport, and Andorra sends a small team to every Olympic Games.
content.history: Legend says the emperor Charlemagne granted Andorra its first charter in the 800s, and the national anthem still praises him. Real records begin in 1278, when a dispute between a French count and the Bishop of Urgell was settled by agreeing to share power over the valleys. That arrangement, with the count's rights passing over time to the French head of state, has lasted more than 700 years, making Andorra one of the oldest continuous states in Europe. For centuries its people farmed, raised sheep, and grew tobacco in isolation. Andorra stayed neutral in both world wars. In 1993 it adopted its first written constitution, giving real power to an elected parliament, and joined the United Nations the same year.
funFacts: Andorra has no airport and no army; France and Spain are responsible for its defense.
The country has one of the longest life expectancies in the world, often placed in the top five.
Andorra la Vella, at over 1,000 meters, is the highest capital city in Europe.
With about eight million visitors a year, tourists outnumber residents roughly a hundred to one.
Andorra's tax-free shops make it a giant open-air mall, and its main avenue is lined with electronics and perfume stores.

content.tagline: From steaming jungle to icy Patagonia
content.overview:
Argentina stretches down the southeastern side of South America for more than 3,500 kilometers, from tropical waterfalls in the north to glaciers and windswept islands near Antarctica. It is the eighth-largest country in the world, about 2.78 million km², roughly four times the size of Texas, with about 46 million people. Its neighbors are Chile, Bolivia, Paraguay, Brazil and Uruguay, and the Atlantic Ocean washes its long eastern coast.

Around a third of Argentines live in and around the capital, Buenos Aires, a huge city of grand avenues, cafes and tango halls on the Río de la Plata. Many families have Italian and Spanish roots, which shows in the food, the accents and the passion for soccer. Spanish is the national language, and Guaraní is also official in the northeastern province of Corrientes.

Argentina is a federal republic with an elected president. Farming and ranching on the vast grasslands called the Pampas have made it one of the world's great producers of beef, wheat and soybeans.
content.landAndNature:
The Andes form Argentina's western wall, crowned by Aconcagua, which at about 6,960 meters is the highest mountain outside Asia. East of the mountains lie the Pampas, flat, fertile grasslands that seem to run forever, and in the south the dry, windy plateau of Patagonia. In the far northeast, the Iguazú Falls thunder over 275 separate cascades on the border with Brazil.

Climate ranges from subtropical heat in the north to freezing cold in Tierra del Fuego, the island at the continent's tip. The Perito Moreno Glacier in Patagonia is famous for the towers of blue ice that crash into Lake Argentino. Wildlife includes guanacos (wild relatives of llamas), rheas, the Andean condor, Magellanic penguins, southern right whales and jaguars in the northern forests.
content.peopleAndCulture:
Argentines speak Spanish with a distinctive rhythm shaped by Italian immigrants, and "che" is a friendly way to get someone's attention. Life revolves around long meals: the asado, a slow barbecue of beef over wood coals, is a weekend ritual, along with empanadas, milanesas and dulce de leche, a caramel spread eaten on everything. Friends share mate, a bitter herbal tea sipped through a metal straw from a gourd.

Soccer is a national obsession, and Diego Maradona and Lionel Messi are treated as heroes after leading the team to World Cup wins in 1986 and 2022. Tango, born in the working-class ports of Buenos Aires in the late 1800s, is the country's signature music and dance. Gauchos, the horse-riding cowboys of the Pampas, remain a proud symbol of rural life.
content.history:
Indigenous peoples such as the Diaguita, Mapuche, Guaraní and Tehuelche lived across the land long before Spanish explorers arrived in the early 1500s. Buenos Aires was permanently founded in 1580, and the region became part of Spain's empire. On May 25, 1810, the people of Buenos Aires set up their own government, and independence was declared in 1816; General José de San Martín then led armies over the Andes to free Chile and Peru as well.

Between 1880 and 1930 millions of Europeans, especially Italians and Spaniards, arrived by ship, and Argentina became one of the richest countries on Earth. The 1900s brought political turmoil, including the popular leader Juan Perón and a military dictatorship from 1976 to 1983 in which tens of thousands of people were kidnapped and killed. After a failed war with Britain over the Falkland Islands, which Argentina calls the Malvinas, democracy returned in 1983.
funFacts: The ballpoint pen was perfected and patented in Argentina in 1943 by László Bíró, a Hungarian immigrant; Argentines still call pens 'biromes.'
In 1892 Argentine police became the first in the world to solve a crime using fingerprints.
Argentinosaurus, one of the largest dinosaurs ever discovered, was found in Patagonia and may have weighed as much as ten elephants.
The country's name comes from argentum, the Latin word for silver, which early explorers hoped to find.
Ushuaia, on Tierra del Fuego, is often called the southernmost city in the world.
Buenos Aires has more bookshops per person than almost any other city on Earth.

content.tagline: An ancient land of stone and apricots
content.overview:
Armenia is a small, mountainous, landlocked country in the Caucasus, the rugged region between the Black Sea and the Caspian Sea where Europe and Asia meet. It borders Georgia, Azerbaijan, Iran and Türkiye. At about 29,700 km² it is roughly the size of Belgium or the US state of Maryland, and about 3 million people live there, with many more Armenians living abroad than at home.

The capital, Yerevan, is one of the oldest continuously inhabited cities in the world, founded as the fortress of Erebuni in 782 BC, decades before Rome. Its buildings are made of pink volcanic stone, and on clear days the snow-capped cone of Mount Ararat, which now lies across the border in Türkiye, fills the southern sky.

Armenia is a republic with an elected parliament and prime minister. Its people are proud of an alphabet, a church and a culture that have survived for more than 1,700 years despite conquests, exile and disaster.
content.landAndNature:
Almost all of Armenia sits above 1,000 meters, and its landscape is a tumble of volcanic plateaus, deep gorges and mountain ranges. Mount Aragats, an extinct volcano of about 4,090 meters, is the highest point. Lake Sevan, one of the largest high-altitude lakes in the world, covers about a twentieth of the country and is known as Armenia's "sea."

Summers are hot and dry, winters cold and snowy. Fields and orchards fill the Ararat Plain, where apricots, grapes and pomegranates ripen in the sun; the Latin name for the apricot, Prunus armeniaca, means "Armenian plum." Bezoar goats, brown bears, wolves and the rare Caucasian leopard live in the mountains, and the Armenian gull nests around Lake Sevan.
content.peopleAndCulture:
Armenian is a language with its own branch of the Indo-European family and its own 39-letter alphabet, created by the monk Mesrop Mashtots in the year 405. Most people belong to the Armenian Apostolic Church, and monasteries carved into cliffs, like Geghard and Tatev, are cherished places. Carved stone crosses called khachkars stand in churchyards all over the country.

Bread is central to every meal: thin lavash is baked against the walls of an underground clay oven, a tradition recognized by UNESCO. Families share dolma, grilled khorovats meat and sweet dried fruit. The duduk, a wooden flute with a haunting sound, is the national instrument. Chess is a required school subject, and Armenia has produced several world-class grandmasters.
content.history:
The kingdom of Urartu ruled these highlands nearly 3,000 years ago, and Armenia's own kings followed. In 301, King Tiridates III made Christianity the state religion, the first country in the world to do so. For centuries afterward, Armenia was fought over by Persians, Romans, Arabs, Mongols, Ottomans and Russians, and Armenians spread out across the Middle East and Europe.

During World War I, in 1915, the Ottoman government deported and killed more than a million Armenians, a tragedy known as the Armenian Genocide. A short-lived independent republic in 1918 was absorbed into the Soviet Union in 1920. Armenia declared independence again in 1991. Since then it has fought Azerbaijan over the region of Nagorno-Karabakh, which Azerbaijan took full control of in 2023, sending most of its Armenian population to Armenia.
funFacts: The world's oldest known leather shoe, about 5,500 years old, was found in Armenia's Areni cave, still laced up.
The same cave held the oldest known winery, where people were pressing grapes about 6,100 years ago.
Since 2011, chess has been a compulsory subject in Armenian primary schools.
The Wings of Tatev cable car, 5.7 kilometers long, set a world record for the longest nonstop reversible aerial tramway when it opened in 2010.
Yerevan is nicknamed the Pink City because its buildings are made of rose-colored volcanic tuff stone.
Roughly three times as many Armenians live outside Armenia as inside it.
